title: In April 2029, an asteroid will slip past Earth closer than our highest satellites

cover.alt: Computer model of the dark, lumpy asteroid Apophis in black space, seen from behind as it heads towards Earth.
cover.credit: NASA/GSFC Scientific Visualization Studio · Public domain

body: On 13 April 2029, the asteroid **Apophis**, a lump of rock a few hundred metres across, will pass about 31,600 km above Earth’s surface: inside the ring of geostationary satellites, and only a tenth of the way to the Moon. No asteroid this big has come so close in recorded history; on average it happens about once every 800 years. Soon after its discovery in 2004, the chance of a 2029 impact was briefly put at 2.7%, the highest rating any object has had on the Torino scale of impact hazards. Later measurements, including radar, ruled out a collision for at least the next 100 years, so the flyby will be a show instead: from dark places in Europe, Africa and western Asia it should be visible to the naked eye.

slides.alt: Computer animation seen from just behind the asteroid Apophis: Earth, first a dark night side dotted with city lights, grows huge behind the rock, swings past in daylight, then shrinks into a small blue ball as the asteroid moves away.
slides.caption: Computer model: riding along with Apophis through 13 April 2029, as Earth looms up behind it, sweeps past and shrinks away again.
slides.credit: NASA/GSFC Scientific Visualization Studio · Public domain · excerpt, cropped

slides.question: How far above Earth’s surface will Apophis pass, in thousands of kilometres?
slides.explanation: About 31,600 km, just under the roughly 35,900 km height of geostationary satellites, and about a tenth of the distance to the Moon.

slides.heading: In late 2004, the odds of Apophis hitting Earth in 2029 were put at 1 in 37 (2.7%)
slides.note: New observations soon ruled out a 2029 impact

events.text: Apophis is discovered at Kitt Peak
A record Torino scale rating of 4
No risk for at least 100 years

slides.question: What should Earth’s gravity do to Apophis as it passes?
options: Capture it as a second moon
slides.explanation: Earth’s pull will move it into a larger orbit and is likely to alter its rotation. NASA’s OSIRIS-APEX spacecraft is due to arrive soon after to study the changes.
